nameStory: Lopadium disciforme doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists stick with its Latin name. The genus name 'Lopadium' comes from the Greek word 'lopadion,' meaning 'little dish,' perfectly describing its cup-shaped fruiting bodies. The species name 'disciforme' means 'disc-shaped,' reinforcing this saucer-like appearance.
description: Lopadium disciforme is a small crustose lichen that forms thin, crusty patches on tree bark and rocks. This tiny organism is actually a partnership between a fungus and algae working together. The lichen body appears as a grayish or whitish crust, often barely noticeable until you spot its distinctive small, dark fruiting discs. Individual patches rarely exceed a few inches across, and the fruiting bodies are typically just 1-2 millimeters wide.

idTips.label: Fruiting discs
idTips.description: Look for tiny, dark brown to black disc-shaped structures that sit flush with or slightly raised above the lichen surface, feeling smooth and slightly glossy when touched with a fingertip

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: The main lichen body feels rough and granular, like fine sandpaper, and may crack or flake when gently scraped with a fingernail

idTips.label: Thin growth form
idTips.description: Forms very thin patches that seem almost painted onto the surface, barely raising above the bark or rock substrate

idTips.label: Grayish coloration
idTips.description: The main body ranges from pale gray to whitish, sometimes with a slight greenish tint when moist

idTips.label: Size and scale
idTips.description: Individual fruiting discs are pinhead-sized, requiring close inspection or a hand lens to see clearly

habitat: This uncommon lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees and occasionally on rocks in older forests throughout New England. It seems to prefer the bark of mature oaks, maples, and birches in relatively undisturbed woodland areas. You're most likely to find it in mid-elevation forests with good air quality, away from heavily polluted areas.

seasonality.spring: The lichen becomes more noticeable as increased moisture brings out its colors and the dark fruiting discs may become more prominent. Spring rains can make the grayish body appear slightly more greenish.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen may appear faded and the crusty surface becomes more brittle and prone to cracking. The dark fruiting discs remain visible and are often the easiest feature to spot.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture revitalizes the lichen, and this is often the best time to observe its characteristics as falling leaves reveal more bark surface. The contrast between the gray lichen and dark discs is most apparent.
seasonality.winter: The lichen remains visible year-round, though it may appear more muted in color. Snow and ice can temporarily obscure it, but it's still identifiable on exposed bark surfaces during warm spells.

funFact: Despite being spotted only six times in New England, this lichen might actually be more common than records suggest – it's so small and inconspicuous that most people walk right past it, mistaking it for a natural stain or discoloration on tree bark!
confusionNotes: This lichen can easily be overlooked as just bark discoloration or confused with other small crustose lichens with dark fruiting bodies. The key is the combination of the very thin, crusty growth and the small, disc-shaped (not cup-shaped) dark fruiting structures that sit nearly flush with the surface.
contextualKnowledge: Like many lichens, Lopadium disciforme is sensitive to air pollution, so finding it can be an indicator of good local air quality. The rarity of recorded observations doesn't necessarily mean it's endangered – it's more likely that this tiny, subtle lichen is simply underreported by citizen scientists.
compareHints: Since this is the only Lopadium species recorded in New England, compare it with other small crustose lichens in the region. Unlike many similar species, Lopadium disciforme has distinctly disc-shaped (not cup-shaped or irregular) fruiting bodies that are dark and sit nearly flush with the lichen surface. The combination of very thin crusty growth and perfectly round, flat, dark discs helps distinguish it from other bark-dwelling crustose lichens.
